In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for error correction, particularly when combined with stabilizer measurements. Utilizing a single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates in parity-check circuits is demonstrated using the toric code, resulting in improved fault tolerance when applying a five-qubit gate over individual two-qubit gates in the context of quantum error correction, particularly when applied to ion qubits susceptible to spontaneous photon scattering, leading to an approximate $40\%$ threshold advantage in the latter case.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most suitable codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the transmitted signal, with only the associated indices and weights needed for feedback. This method simplifies channel estimation and performance evaluation, as the mobile terminal doesn't need to estimate the channel, and only a few bits are exchanged for encoding the selected codebook entries. This approach is particularly beneficial for frequency division duplexing due to limited uplink channel access.

A type of current, known as nonequilibrium surface current, can flow around the edges of a two-dimensional material under specific conditions. These conditions involve a complex relationship between the Hofstadter spectrum and lattice resonance and are robust against disordered systems. Our research into a three-dimensional Hofstadter model reveals that this type of current is prevalent within slabs of a cubic lattice and can be found in multiple layers. By introducing a magnetic field, we are able to map this three-dimensional scenario onto a two-dimensional system with a resonant vacuum SCQW, allowing us to theoretically calculate and validate our findings through sample calculations and scalar and vector disorder scenarios. Our results confirm that the surface currents flow in opposite directions on the top and bottom faces of the slab and can extend to additional internal layers under certain conditions. By analyzing pump-probe conductivity, we determine that this type of current can be detected experimentally.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical method for early galaxy evolution. Our approach tracks the development of such remnants across various mass scales and chemical compositions, taking into account their formation rates, mass ratios, and distance from cluster centers. Our model predicts significant gravitational wave activity as these remnants merge in nuclear star clusters in the first billion years of a galaxy's history. Specifically, significant observable signals will come from neutron star black hole and double black hole mergers, which experience a higher probability of such events outside cluster centers due to lower gravitational wave probabilities experienced there.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid cathode fluorescent X-ray tube paired with a high-voltage generator. This portable GRB simulator has been successfully demonstrated with it producing a simulated all-sky burst which was detected by both GECAM and other satellite GRBs all-sensors, including the Chinese Gamma-ray Large Area Area Telescope (LAT), the Italian-Dutch Gamma-ray Burst Telescope (GBI) on board the Integral and X-ray Telescope (XRT) on board the Swift satellites respectively.  Additionally, this study examines how the parameters of the simulator such as its voltage, exposure time and grid settings can be used to customize its output and produce grand bursts which may correspond to specific types of Gamma-Ray Bursts and their afterglows as well as binary mergers that produce gravitational waves.  This research indicates that the proposed simulator meets the requirements of detecting GRBs and classifying them based on certain features which can aid multi-messenger astronomy in identifying possible candidates for detecting GRBs that are

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with its scientific productivity. This study aims to examine the relationship between the amount of knowledge within a scientific field and its associated productivity. By mining the abstracts and headings from the entire corpus of scientific publications, categorized by International Patent Classification, this research estimates the knowledge amount within each patent class, and subsequently compares it to the number of patents granted. Analyzing 2.3 million patents from 1970 to 2010, the study found that greater knowledge amounts within specific classes generally lead to increased productivity. Nevertheless, this relationship varies significantly, demonstrating substantial disproportion within the scientific community. Notably, industries exhibiting high proportions between scientific productivity and knowledge amount tend to be foundational, demonstrating diverse applications. This research further implies that breakthroughs in science and technology are most likely to transpire in such multifaceted domains.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to non-trivial topology of the underlying lattice have been successfully employed to transport particles without scattering. Incorporating a localized quantum impurity into such a system enables a single particle sector to be represented by Jaynes-Cummings model, while interaction between the impurity and conduction electrons generates a shifted charge on the impurity, known as the Friedel moment, both of which are influenced by the system's topological properties. Notably, an integer quantum Hall system exhibits distinct even-odd symmetry in its symmetry breaking, and successfully switches the Friedel moment from near zero to four units of charge as the Fermi energy is positioned on either side of the mobility gap. Successful predictions were also made for both quantities in graphene and silicene, albeit with different values. Additionally, placing the quantum impurity at a special high-symmetry point in graphene and silicene modifies the resonance profile, and this modification varies depending on the number of filled bands.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FD-FBM is created by combining advanced LSTM variations and the hFactorizedBackprop method. In addition, a factorized weight representation is used to reduce the number of parameters and enable precise updates during training. The proposed factorized approach is also compatible with fixed-point precisions, further enhancing its efficiency. Furthermore, a new hardware architecture called HLTLS is created to accelerate these advanced LSTM structures through the use of tensor cores and custom-designed hardware components optimized for high-performance, low-power operations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform existing algorithms and hardware designs in terms of accuracy and efficiency when applied to high-accuracy video recognition tasks.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP models' performance in data-scarce environments, data augmentation techniques have been widely investigated in the last decade. A thorough examination of data augmentation techniques in NLP has been lacking until now, as existing surveys either cover only specific applications or domains, or concentrate on techniques without considering their effectiveness in various settings. Our study fills this gap by presenting the first comprehensive investigation of data augmentation techniques in NLP, encompassing applications across text classification, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, question answering, and natural language understanding. We highlight the importance of selecting suitable baselines when evaluating the efficacy of augmentation techniques and present recommendations for conducting rigorous experiments in NLP data augmentation studies.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is rooted in the idea that gravity should not be the longest-range force. We make the case for formulating the Weak Gravity Conjecture in a conformal field theory based on its property of dividing charged operators into two categories: those that exhibit exponential growth as they move across a geodesic in the theory's space, and those that grow at a rate no faster than polynomially. We then provide several examples and theoretical principles that support the hypothesis that a valid ECJ exists for a broad spectrum of conformal field theories, including uncharged, partially charged, and exponentially charged theories. We also discuss the connection between exponentially charged theories and their corresponding sigma models, as well as their behavior under the process of renormalization group flow.

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension and we consider a specific interval of integers, the condition for $F$-rationality is equivalent to an inequality involving that lower bound and then to the equality of that inequality and the tight Hilbert function for that interval of integers. These conditions can be expanded to include conditions on the tight Hilbert distribution and the dualizing module of that ideal. If the ring is two-dimensional and we consider specific values for its integers, the condition for $F$-rationality is equivalent to the regularity of that dualizing module and a specific value for its coefficient, which specifically holds true for those specific values for its integers. These conditions can be extended to include conditions on the tight Hilbert distribution and the values of that dualizing module.

The rapid advancement of electricity system components is necessitating a reevaluation of regulatory policies. Electric system operators are facing increased pressure to coordinate market interactions and prevent supply-demand imbalances. This paper introduces Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM), a new tool for evaluating electricity market reforms. ASAM employs generalized equilibrium concepts to examine how changes in regulation influence market behavior. It is based on block responsiveness analysis and incorporates the challenge of electricity market operations through unit commitment models. This approach enables comparative statics to be applied to endogenous decision-making processes without assuming market participants' strategies are perfectly predictable. The ASAM framework is used to analyze the impact of reducing generation costs on reliability services and the effects of policy modifications on market outcomes.

R.C. Vaughan initially studied the conditions under which an irreducible polynomial f(x), when composed with another polynomial g(x), maintains its irreducibility. This composition irredcibility property was later linked to prime iterates in integers by I. Kapranov. We establish a connection that allows us to obtain precise criteria ensuring the irreducibility of primality cases when Lefschetz zeta functions are involved. This approach yields the irreducibility of specific polynomial compositions such as the Coxeter-Lyndon prime iterates, the Lemmermeyer prime iterates, the Solé-Wada-Suzuki prime iterates, the Muratov prime iterates, the Muratov-Cohen prime iterates, the Muratov-Sole-Wada prime iterates, the Muratov-Muratov prime iterates, the Muratov-Muratov-Cohen prime iterates, and the Muratov-Muratov-Sole-Wada prime iterates, when the underlying polynomial has an irreducible form. This framework also provides novel irreducibility proofs for a broader class of polynomial compositions including the Muratov prime iterates, the Muratov-Cohen prime iterates, the Muratov-Sole-Wada prime iterates, the Muratov-Muratov prime iterates, the Muratov-Muratov-Cohen prime iterates, and the Muratov-Muratov-Sole-Wada prime iterates, assuming the irreduc

To enhance experimental searches for the Higgs boson pair production through non-resonant processes, particularly in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel, this work demonstrates the effectiveness of the matrix element method. By comparing simulated parton level events to real data from the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, an accurate measurement of the normalized differential cross-sections was obtained for specific differential distributions, including the Higgs diphoton invariant mass, the lepton transverse momentum, and the missing transverse energy. The measured results closely matched both the theoretical predictions and real ATLAS data with a reduced chi-square value close to one. In comparison, parton shower Monte Carlo simulations were less accurate in reproducing these results, indicating that the matrix element method provides a more precise description of $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ events and could potentially enhance the sensitivity of experimental searches for Higgs boson pair production.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 by future e+e- colliders due to precise measurements of σ(e+e- → Zh) that complement searches for the Standard Model scalar sector at particle colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider, or a possible future pp collider, or Higgs decay to photons. We also find the sensitivity of σ(e+e- → Zh) and γγ decays of the Higgs boson to have the most notable complementary role in the complex triplet model scenario.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations, with a significant temperature disparity between summer and winter. In the high summer, the polar atmosphere is heated by sunlight reflected from methane clouds below, forming a warm seasonal polar vortex. Conversely, the long winter results in the accumulation of shadow and the formation of a deep polar night. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, solutions with symmetric states and positive energy will also exhibit the same blow-up behavior found in the entire space. These findings extend previous results by demarcating conditions under which solutions with positive energy exhibit finite time collapse, thereby contributing to the understanding of this particular phenomenon.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, and our findings indicate that the metal-insulator transition is significantly impeded by the presence of an insulating surface layer as the system transitions from one surface termination to another.  Moreover, our comparative analysis of the effect of surface termination on the metal-insulator transition utilized core-level spectroscopy and Hamiltonian inverse problem solving, and our findings indicate that the intermediate layer between the metal oxide core and the surface termination has the most substantial and direct impact on the metal-insulator transition.  Understanding the metal-insulator transition will be significantly facilitated by a thorough investigation of the effect of surface termination on the electronic structure, as our studies and future ones with varying degrees of stoichiometry demonstrated that a distorted intermediate layer, caused by interfacial strain, hinders the understanding of the metal-insulator transition.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle, and then demonstrate the construction of the inverse of this functor. This allows for the representation of k-fold vector bundles as graded bundles of degree k within the same category. Additionally, we establish the conditions for the existence of alternating and symmetric multi-vector fields on graded bundles, and show that these conditions are equivalent to specific symmetries in their transformation laws. This facilitates the development of alternative approaches to defining symmetry within the context of Lagrangian systems defined on graded bundles.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to gather information about a sample's molecular, atomic, or atomic-nuclear components. Although being scattered by a sample, the light or x-rays being used can have their phase and amplitude altered, yet this data is crucial for reconstructing the sample's properties through complex algorithms in coherent scattering techniques. However, in the case of non-resonant x-ray scattering, which involves a large number of photons, a different approach can yield immediate and direct information, bypassing the need for complex retrieval algorithms. We show that by utilizing linear spectroscopy with x-rays at energy levels matching the nuclear transition of the sample, which consists of hafnium carbide, real-space reconstruction of the sample's crystal structure using small-angle x-ray scattering yields extraordinary results when combined with a simple model fit. This demonstrates the potential of such an approach to provide direct and detailed information, even in situations involving extremely small samples or when only a portion of the data is accessible due to the limitations of detection technologies.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop an effective classical scenario by analyzing how the circuit noise interacts and leads to stochastic local fields representing the distribution of measurement and gate errors. This effective model preserves the disordered nature of the original circuit and maintains connections to its physical parameters and error thresholds. The research focuses on locally connected hypergraphs representing the parity check measurements in the surface code, showing distinct phases like dynamic order, clustered ferromagnetism, and clustering glass in the presence of two-qubit errors. When circuit operations are considered, new dynamic clusters emerge, leading to a new phase, dynamic ferromagnetism, and corresponding threshold, around a two-qubit error case cluster glass. The study also identifies another threshold, the double cluster glass, and its associated phase transition, reflecting a specific two-cluster competition. The associated dynamic order parameter in this threshold is linked to the emergence of long-range correlations in parity check measurements.

Recent theoretical predictions have suggested that topologically non-trivial configurations might be attainable in two-layered 2D group-IV elemental structures, specifically in tellurene. To validate this intriguing possibility, we investigated single-layer tellurene, exploring its stability, electronic characteristics, and topological nature. By applying various corrections and theories, our study discovered that functionalizing tellurene with fluorine or hydroxyl groups enhances its stability and creates large-gap 2D toroidal insulators in contrast to its pristine state. Of note is that these strained monolayers exhibit exceptional in-plane binding energies comparable to those observed in analogous two-dimensional elemental structures based on silicon, germanium, and tin. Interestingly, in comparison to the pristine state where a minimal vacuum gap exists, materials with enhanced stability display minimal closable gaps only under intense strain conditions, indicating promising potential applications.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with arbitrary complex configurations of both fracture types. We establish a fully discrete inf-sup condition for our method in $d$ dimensions and demonstrate convergence rates that are optimal relative to both the discretization and dimensionality of the problem. This approach leverages efficient and highly parallelizable hybrid-dimensional discretization techniques, enabling our theoretical findings to be practically applicable.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics that may arise from inherent or induced magnetic arrangements. Key elements of this research are examined, which include an in-depth analysis of the superconducting state using the Eilenberger theory and a theoretical calculation of the spinTRAP effect. This phenomenon occurs when a spiral magnetic arrangement interacts with a superconducting gap, altering the critical temperature. Ultimately, several design concepts are proposed for optimizing the performance of this innovative device architecture.

Hypothesis evaluation through Bayes Factors is a widely recognized method,
yet its limitations in reliability and comparability across different scenarios
remain prevalent. Our exploration delves into enhancing its consistency by
examining the influence of prior settings and participant counts on Bayes Factor
behavior. Building on previous research, our approach expands upon a Monte Carlo
simulation framework to incorporate real data into Bayes Factor calculations,
however this aspect is left for future investigation. Our comprehensive analysis
has led to the creation of visual tools such as Bayes Factor Heatmaps and Ensembles,
which facilitate the identification of reliable Bayes Factor conclusions. Ultimately,
introducing a process for validating statistically significant hypotheses based on
Bayes Factors, our proposal involves utilizing additional, unrelated datasets to
confirm initial hypotheses. This concept can be viewed as a foundational element
for developing robust statistical workflows involving Bayes Factor theory.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate how pre-trained language models comprehend discourse relationships. Existing methods rely on extensive training for prediction, but the current method requires minimal training and is capable of projecting a broad range of discourse relationships. The proposed technique has been tested on several languages and demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy compared to existing baselines.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated a significant carrier activation energy.  This value was found to be around 0.4 electron volts, which implies a very limited carrier activation rate in diamond with low defect concentrations, as typically used in quantum applications.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, mimicking an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model with p-box symmetry. Taking a large-p limit, they found the model reduces to a relativistic sigma model in three-dimensional space, described by the SU(3)/U(1)^2 manifold. Due to a non-trivial homotopy, this model possesses distinct magnetic vortices, or skyrmions, that can be excised, leaving behind stable, deconfined anyons with semilocal charges. A perturbative analysis of perturbations revealed the semilocal string's tension to be composed of two components - a perturbative part and a non-perturbative part arising from semilocal skyrmion deformation - thus explaining a possible mechanism behind the confinement semilocal charges. A detailed analysis of perturbations' self-interactions yielded insights into the semilocal string's tension expansion, verifiable through lattice simulations.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to the varying functional states found in both artificial and natural complex systems. Researchers will utilize a recently developed, broadly applicable model to analyze second-order dynamics in self-sustaining oscillator systems, which comprises different types of interconnections between the oscillators. Through this model, they will establish a definitive criterion that distinguishes between system states based solely on the pattern of connections, applicable to various types of networks. Furthermore, they will apply this criterion to investigate the instability leading to sudden collective behavior in complex systems, taking into account a wide range of interconnection types within different networks, as well as oscillators with different stabilities. Predicted indicators of system-wide instability derived from this approach will be compared with those obtained from existing theories concerning the more narrowly defined dynamics of specific networks. Lastly, simulations involving multiple types of interconnections within the model will demonstrate its superiority over traditional models that consider only mean connections within populations of interdependent oscillator systems.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large neighborhoods of global minima. We propose analyzing its global landscape in two parts: local minima vs. global minima. We demonstrate that under a perturbation of the geodesic curvature, any local minimum is equivalent to any global minimum. These results are relevant for evaluating first-order methods and provide a comprehensive factorization approach to analyze the landscape, including regions with minima and strict saddles. We apply these findings to various loss functions, including logistic regression, support vector machines, and robust regression with Huber loss, as well as matrix completion and low-rank representation problems. We also discuss implications for representations that are not isometric.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed by a researcher named Faudree, with an yet unresolved lower limit set at five colors for edge coloring in bipartite graphs. The current study presents the first example for a class of bipartite graphs that necessitate at least seven colors, specifically within the family of bipartite graphs that can be divided into two equal subsets with a total of 42 edges.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and relic density place very high limits, up to EeV, on these particles' mass. To derive more precise constraints, this study introduces a model involving unstable particles that decouple after electroweak symmetry breaking. It also considers particles that form Kugelblitzes or long-lasting strings-particles resonances, which could influence structure formation in the early universe. By applying semi-classical reasoning to this model, derived constraints from various universe observations are significantly reduced, taking into account particles' abundance generated during the universe's history.

Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that the influence is dictated by a competition between two, viscoelastic-related asymmetries, which vary according to the swapper body and helical tail configuration, and ultimately can be governed by a single parameter of front-back asymmetry. Moreover, our study reveals that the impact is most pronounced in swimmers with highly asymmetric distributions of surface force oscillations, and in viscoelastic conditions, they may even exhibit directionality in their swimming movement.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social learning" through exposure to market outcomes and past production decisions, we found the algorithm successfully converged to the Nash Equilibrium in a standard symmetric Cournot game with a linear inverse demand function and constant marginal costs. Furthermore, the resulting convergence rate was significantly improved relative to the results obtained by Rubinstein (1986) in his analysis of repeated play under perfect recall.

The growing threat landscape necessitates enhanced cybersecurity monitoring, 
where threat intelligence sources like Common Platform Information Model (CPMI) 
can be utilized to identify and mitigate new threats effectively. Despite their 
potential, extracting security-relevant information from natural language 
security threats within CMI requires addressing challenges posed by the structured 
nature of the data format. This study proposes a novel approach to incorporate 
insightful security attributes into CMI by leveraging state-of-the-art deep 
learning techniques and adapting its output to align with CMI's unique data 
structure, ultimately aiding in more informed security decision-making processes.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering.

The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had previously been considered intractable. Despite their profound advantages, reliable estimation of uncertainty associated with predictions remains a significant challenge. Traditional machine learning approaches受限于 grappling with reliable uncertainty estimation associated with complex predictions, particularly when it comes to predicting relatively well-understood phenomena from poorly defined inputs. This challenge is further complicated by machine learning models such as neural operator trained on limited data and subject to various sources of noise, necessitating uncertainty assessment not only at the level of data but also at the level of predictions. This paper provides an extensive quantitative analysis of the effectiveness of various methods designed to address these uncertainty challenges. Specifically, this study carefully compares a range of techniques focused on quantifying both input-level and prediction-level uncertainties associated with parameters such as boundary conditions, physical fields, and temporal evolution within dynamic systems modeled by partial differential equations. This investigation encompasses comparative assessments of Bayesian neural networks, Monte Carlo dropout, ensemble methods, and confidence prediction techniques such as IQRA, RTP, and IQNU, yielding insightful recommendations for effectively addressing and reducing uncertainty in domains of scientific machine learning.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.
Using an exact partition function, we analyze a unitary matrix model based on a single plaquette configuration at a finite $N$ for both the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Realizing the full potential of these models requires ensuring their computational robustness. However, traditional approaches to verifying CNN correctness are computationally expensive and lack interpretability. This work aims to address these challenges by introducing an method to assess the safety case for activation range supervision in hardware-fault-tolerant CNNs, leveraging both statistical and non-statistical analysis techniques. This approach combines ANNs simulation data with static data analytics to evaluate the reliability of range-supervised tolerance methods against multiple robustness metrics under varied testing conditions. Initially, a simulation is used to measure the actual accuracy and expected tolerance of a standard CNN when confronted with corrupted input data. Next, we compare this performance with that of hardware-based fault tolerance methods, including binarization, quantization, and round-to-nearest rounding, to determine the efficacy of their range-supervised counterparts.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual number of transactions can be reduced to just one, saving on transaction costs. Given that this process significantly impacts a country's economy, the development of efficient netting or clearing systems, tailored to local characteristics, becomes crucial. These can be implemented in various government sectors, including ministries of finance, trade, and industry, as well as specialized institutions like national netting centers. In this paper, we introduce a novel graph-based algorithm capable of efficiently calculating netting solutions for government institutions and present its application within the Romanian Ministry of Economy. Additionally, we compare our approach to other established graph-based techniques.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters maintains a consistent meaning across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level patterns, and linguistic properties, which can be incorporated as necessary. We employ a novel ensemble learning technique to construct this cross-lingual semantic space, leveraging our findings about word clusters. Our results show substantial gains in machine translation, categorization, and language translation tasks, outperforming the use of single-language word spaces and recently developed multilingual embedding techniques.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in mid-central Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV has been 
reported here. The particle yields were determined from momentum spectra in 
specific transverse momentum ranges, allowing for the calculation of ratios 
between these particles and the particle-to-proton ratio, which indicated the 
latter to be nearly twice as much as in Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy. 
Additionally, by analyzing the distribution of proton $p_T$, a new 
transverse baryon number rapidity profile had been defined for these collisions, 
and also the centrality dependence of particle production had been investigated. 
Measurements of the aforementioned, combined with previous data, offered insight 
into the formation and evolution of the produced matter. Furthermore, 
comparing the results to theoretical models revealed the need for an enhanced 
production of protons in the central region of the produced medium.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 16 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within a specific margin of error, although we note that the particular line and wavelength range used may affect the accuracy. Furthermore, we find that the predictions are most accurate when using a specific range of wavelengths, which supports existing research on the topic.

We are studying a critical boundary where polynomials that are sums of squares suddenly cease to represent all other polynomials of the same degree and degree three in multiple variables. This specific boundary is known as the convex cone of nonnegative polynomials. A notable example, Hilbert's second inequality, illustrates that beyond certain variables, this boundary suddenly expands to include polynomials that are not sums of squares. We focus on a specific plane within this cone boundary and identify three critical points where sums of squares positivity is lost. We also examine the nature of this type of boundary expansion, particularly in relation to its geometric properties and its relationship to other parts of this cone boundary.

In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish three key constraints: the conservation of lepton number, the distinct masses of flavor eigenstates, and a new conservation law, which we term "triuity," required for three-neutrino oscillations to occur. We examine the consequences of violating or satisfying these constraints, focusing on specific cases such as equality of neutrino masses or complete absence of oscillations. We also analyze a new experiment, FASER$\nu$, located at CERN, that will provide the most accurate measurements of neutrino cross-sections at the energy levels relevant for reaching the FASER II detector. We demonstrate that the outcomes of these multiple constraints can be utilized to place the most stringent constraints possible on any model containing more than three neutrino states.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable regular expressions.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO (DVIO) ones, offer the potential to provide precise and consistent localization. However, the application of DVIO in real-world scenarios is hindered by current frameworks that struggle with complex interactions of observations, especially when processing high-dimensional data. To overcome this limitation, we present EMA-VIO, a new framework combining an external memory attention mechanism with VIO, allowing the implicit factor graph to effectively process and integrate observations and constraints for optimal state estimation. By adapting the multi-head external memory attention mechanism, our framework successfully models complex interactions and enhances both positioning accuracy and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements, including up to an 8-fold reduction in running time and up to 2-fold improvement in accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art DVIO algorithms on public benchmarks.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which is a well-established phenomenon. Our non-linear higher-order Weyl model provides a unique combination of both nonlinear effects and the topological properties of the VHM phase. We demonstrate the emergence of both Fermi-arc and higher-order arc states resulting from the interaction between nonlinear wave packet dynamics and topological phenomena. Calculations of both the conventional multipole invariant and a newly proposed nonlinear invariant, the diagonal multipole invariant, confirm the topological nature of the proposed Hamiltonian. Moreover, we show that light absorption induced by two-photon processes in materials hosting fermi arcs will be directly proportional to their connecting arcs' thickness, thus linking optical responses to the topological properties of materials and opening up new avenues for both theoretical and experimental investigations.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to confidentiality concerns, choose not to share their models. To address this issue, we propose the FedSA challenge, a new benchmark challenge in the realm of knowledge amalgamation. It is our belief that FedSA will catalyze the development of innovative research methods for combining models from disparate sources, as exchanging model information is often more beneficial than exchanging training data. To initiate the research on FedSA, we have made the public access to privately accessible training datasets from six industry partners across three domains, as well as six powerful teacher models that have been trained by notable organizations including IBM, Toyota Research Institute, and Amazon Web Services.

Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifespan, its rotation undergoes significant changes, which can be categorized into three distinct stages. During the first stage, its overall rotation slows down as it reaches the main sequence. A significant fraction of solar-type stars, however, exhibit either very rapid or very little rotation. This research focuses on a third category - solar-type stars with moderate, solar-like rotation rates. These stars, often referred to as golden main sequence stars, are typically surrounded by heavy dust envelopes that impede our understanding of their rotational behavior. Consequently, classifications based on rotation rates should also consider the influence of dust on magnetic field activity. Moreover, stars with minimal rotation rates are generally more active, while those with rapid rotation rates are typically less active. This correlation does not hold true for stars surrounded by heavy dust. To explore the potential for such a relationship, our study conducts sophisticated three-dimensional simulations of the dynamic processes at work in solar-type stars and analyzes their average magnetic field patterns. Specifically, we investigate how various rotational speeds affect the magnetic activity and fluctuations of magnetic fields in these stars. Our simulations reveal that increasing rotational speeds lead to greater magnetic activity and more significant magnetic field fluctuations, while also producing periodic magnetic field fluctuations that could correspond to magnetic cycles. However, these effects are nullified when the most intense turbulent motions begin to dominate. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions.

A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum, our research finds that membrane worldsheet catatrasers in dual gravitational theories can violate this limit, specifically under conditions where a significant portion of an entangled region transforms into a disordered state due to a moving spacetime pier. This finding demonstrates that while entropy increase can be significantly amplified by the change in quantum state, there are underlying constraints on uncontrolled quantum dynamics that could serve as a foundation for quantum thermodynamics, including the study of irreversible entropy generation and heat dissipation, especially in extreme conditions such as those present in quark-gluon plasma and early universe plasma.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm.

Consider a unit cube $Q$ embedded in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$. If a function $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{k,\infty}(Q)$, its norm can be bounded by an $s$-th root of $n$ times a constant $C_k$ specific to $k$, multiplied by the norm of an interpolation projector $P_n$ on a given net $\alpha$ within $Q$ consisting of $n$ points. This research aims to determine the best possible value for the constant involving $n$ for various values of $k$ within the range $1\le k\le [d/2]$. Ultimately, the study derives a upper bound for this constant that decreases at a rate of $n^{-(s-(d-1)/s)}$. The lower bound for the $n$-dependence of this constant is also established for functions $f$ that are polynomials of degree $s$.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices.

This study employs a motivic perspective to examine twisted algebraic $K$-theory.
For a variety over a zero-characteristic field and an Azumaya algebra over that
variety, we develop the first twisted motivic spectrum representing $K$-theory in a
stably equivalent way. This representation allows us to derive representability
properties, exact localization, and change-of-varieties sequences. As a result,
we obtain inductive formulas for computing the algebraic $K$-theory of finite
dimensional Azumaya algebras over a point, achieving this using only a base field's
Milnor $K$-theory and its shifts, rather than $GL_n$-homotopy types.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how atmospheric changes are influenced by various internal and external factors. Key processes, including the photodissociation of water, hydrogen and oxygen escape from the upper atmosphere, surface interactions, and the escape of carbon compounds from above the atmosphere, are analyzed using basic physical principles. A simplified mathematical model incorporates these processes and their opposing effects to investigate the mechanisms that may have led to Venus's current atmosphere. It is suggested that, in its early history as a "Wet Venus," with an abundant surface water supply, certain amounts of surface water could have stabilized the atmosphere before eventually becoming "Dry Venus" as surface water sources were depleted. A new concept, "Semi-Habitability," is introduced to describe intermediate atmospheric conditions of interest. Furthermore, a potential scenario is proposed in which specific outgassing rates and initial water amounts on the early Venus surface could have resulted in semi-habitable atmospheric conditions, lasting for an extended period.

Investigating the chemistry occurring on charged droplets offers valuable insights into enhancing industrial chemical production methods, a phenomenon common in nature. To address this, researchers have developed a novel method using reaction nanoscopy on charged propanediol nanodroplets. By leveraging ultrashort laser pulses, they have established the capability to monitor the droplet's average size, charge distribution, and surrounding near-field. Furthermore, they have demonstrated the sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing two types of propanediol isomers, revealing that certain conditions produce a significantly increased yield of methyl ions. Simulation results indicate that this increase results from an optimal molecular alignment on the droplet's surface in one isomer, paving the way for the observation of charge dynamics and chemical reactions within droplets.

Recent breakthroughs in numerical computation, driven by GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly scaled tensor network algorithms for complex quantum simulation and machine learning applications. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which can leverage true quantum hardware for enhanced performance by combining quantum processors with tensor networks. Specifically, recent research has demonstrated that matrix product states can be efficiently decomposed into shallow quantum circuits equivalent to PQC parameterizations. Our key contribution lies in extending this work by developing parametrized product states encompassing non-neural tensor variants, enabling the derivation of efficient decompositions into shallow quantum circuits with O(blogb) depth for block-encoded tensors of bond dimension b. The proposed framework facilitates seamless integration of true quantum processors into tensor network algorithms such as variational matrix product uniform state optimization, while also providing theoretical bounds on circuit depth for replicated states and suggesting optimization strategies for common optimization landscapes.

The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care planning relies heavily on the properties of tissues visible under a microscope. Understanding how cells and tissues interact, depicted in digital pathology images, requires breaking down complex scenes into manageable components and establishing hierarchical relationships. This work aims to provide a framework for creating graph representations that reflect the multi-level nature of these interactions. Our proposed approach involves two steps: a data-driven method to extract graph sub-units using machine learning and a custom algorithm to connect these units at different levels of organization. We tested our approach on pathology images, showcasing its effectiveness through improved cancer detection rates and more accurate predictions when combined with existing detection methods.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this research leads to implications for the convergence rates of sequential Bayesian methods. We have also developed and analyzed an adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for sampling from the posterior, and provided simulation results comparing the performance of this method with existing alternatives.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential to reduce this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small due to a high number of unlabeled images. This research focuses on combining semi-supervised learning with domain adaptation to accommodate variations within and between scanners. We develop a novel contrastive semi-supervised domain adaptive approach called Contrastive SSL for Domain Adaptation (CS2DA). CS2DA leverages a new contrastive loss function that aligns similar anatomical features across domain images, allowing for consistent training across datasets with varying levels of annotation and domain adaptation. The method is particularly suitable for segmenting organs with consistent shapes, such as the liver, across similar anatomical regions. Excellent results are achieved on multiple datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of CS2DA in combining domain adaptation and semi-supervised learning.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all dimensions. Although the issue is well-known, the formalism is still widely employed due to the complexity of obtaining correct results in more realistic scenarios. A modified, defective formula has been derived, and the corresponding gauge symmetry transformation has been demonstrated to function properly within the context of supergravity.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely proportional to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems.

Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+e^-$ collisions between 2 and 6 TeCentered, we consider the impact of recent data. By leveraging the LHC's $\tau$-pair production at 13 TeCentered, we derive a 95% confidence level constraint on the weak process $\tau^+\tau^-$ production at the International Linear Collider (ILC) with 50 GeCentered center-of-mass energy and 0.1 pb intensity. The new $\tau$-pair data from the LHC has significantly tightened the $d_\tau$-search constraints by a factor of three. Specifically, we now know that $|d_\tau(s)| < 2.6 \times 10^{-12} \frac{e}{4\pi m_\tau^2}$ (95% C.L.). With an upgraded detector at the LHC, we can improve this $\tau$-specific constraint to $|d_\tau(s)| < 8.6 \times 10^{-13} \frac{e}{4\pi m_\tau^2}$ (95% C.L.).
